item.title: GeoAI 2027 Conference announcement, TomTom Webinar on site selection analysis, TESSERA embeddings openly available on AWS, Development Seed’s Satellite Embeddings Primer
item.description: GeoAI resources from the GeoAI Research Center at Ghent University, TomTom, and dClimate.
item.dc:creator: Eric van Rees
item.content:encoded:
Resource 1: Announcement of the 2nd International Conference on Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI 2027)

Following the successful GeoAI 2026 Conference in Ghent, Belgium (4–6 June), a second edition has been announced for 2027 in London. The dates are 29 June - 2 July. A conference website is now online, announcing the conference theme “SpaceTimeAI: Bringing Time into GeoAI”.

GeoAI 2026 was organized by the GeoAI Research Center at Ghent University, and brought together 305 conference participants from 36 countries and regions. The GeoAI Research Center is dedicated to advancing the field of geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) through cutting-edge research and collaborative efforts. More info is available on the “About Us” page of the Research Center.

GeoAI Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

If you check the conference page of 2026, you can read that GeoAI 2028 will be hosted by East China Normal University (ECNU, China, represented by Jonathan Li and Min Liu) in Shanghai in 2028. On that page you can also find all online proceedings of the first event, including conference papers and more. Presentation slides are available here. Read a short conference recap here.

Below is the announcement of next year’s conference on LinkedIn, published last week:

Resource 2: TomTom Webinar: Geospatial intelligence in site selection modeling and AI agent building

On September 30, TomTom organized an online webinar titled “Geospatial intelligence in site selection modeling and AI agent building”. It provides a technical deep dive to learn how geospatial intelligence powers modern site selection workflows and how to build and evaluate a Site Selection Agent using TomTom Maps SDK, Agent toolkit and Embeddings. If you’ve been following my earlier Substack articles, you know that Geolytix and CARTO have similar offerings for site selection.

The webinar ends with a 10-minute Q&A with some great questions from the audience, covering topics such as

  • training and finetuning site selection models,

  • controlling LLM inference costs,

  • how map embeddings are used with agents, and

  • bringing in user datasets into the toolkit runtime.

Rewatch the webinar here.

Resource 3: TESSERA embeddings are now openly available on AWS

TESSERA is a foundation model for Earth observation developed at the University of Cambridge. TESSERA is an acronym for Temporal Embeddings of Surface Spectra for Earth Representation and Analysis. The excellent TESSERA project website contains news, blog posts, videos, and more.

Cambridge University published an official release of the foundation model on 4 June 2026, which is available here.

Matt Forrest discussed the usability of TESSERA in a LinkedIn post, stating it is good for a quick check, but not as a replacement for a trained model:

More news on TESSERA from dClimate, the world’s first decentralized, blockchain-based marketplace and intelligence ecosystem for climate and weather data. dClimate’s website has a lot of resources on geographic embeddings, including TESSERA. dClimate published a recent article announcing that TESSERA’s global Earth observation embeddings are now openly available on AWS (available here).

This recently published article provides a general-audience look at what the open-source foundation model TESSERA can do. It is meant as a background to the TESSERA AWS release.

Resource 4: Development Seed’s Primer for Earth Data Embeddings

Development Seed published a primer for Earth Data Embeddings. This 10-minute read explains what are embeddings, what you can do with them, how to interpret them and what’s next for embeddings. Check out the visuals that illustrate the text and the links for more information. All in all a great introduction to satellite embeddings. Read the announcement post on LinkedIn with additional links.

That’s it for this week!

item.title: WeatherNext 3, AlphaEarth Foundations Custom Satellite Embeddings, and AI Architecture Terminology Explained
item.dc:creator: Eric van Rees
item.content:encoded:
September has been pretty amazing so far regarding GeoAI news. What stands out for me is WeatherNext 3, which is Google Deepmind and Google Research’s AI weather model that offers prediction at unprecedented resolution. Next up is Custom Satellite Embeddings from AlphaEarth Foundations, announced this summer. Third is …

Resource 1: WeatherNext 3 announcement

The announcement of WeatherNext 3, the latest AI weather model from Google, received a lot of attention. Google published an extensive blog announcing the release, followed by coverage elsewhere, including an excellent write-up on TechCrunch.

GeoAI Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Google calls “it the most advanced and accurate global weather model to date”, that uses raw satellite data to produce a forecast every hour in high resolution to make reliable forecasts accessible across Google products worldwide. WeatherNext 3 provides a global weather picture roughly five times sharper than its previous model, WeatherNext 2.

Google’s Yossi Matias announced the release on LinkedIn in the following post, where he points out that the AI model introduces specific forecasts for 100-meter wind speeds, cloud cover, and sun radiation to assist global clean energy planning and grid operations. Why grid balancing needs better forecasts is explained here.

I asked Gemini if it’s possible to combine data from WeatherNext 3 and AlphaEarth Foundations, and this is indeed possible:

Resource 2: AlphaEarth Foundations Custom Satellite Embeddings

In July 2026, Google announced Custom Satellite Embeddings, that complement its existing Satellite Embeddings dataset released in 2025. The announcement reads as follows:

“Custom Satellite Embeddings are flexible, on-demand embeddings that allow organizations to transition from annual mapping to monitoring and change detection for custom time periods and regions of interest. This new data product from Google Maps Platform complements our global annual Satellite Embedding dataset in Earth Engine and Google Cloud Storage, by providing higher-frequency, on-demand data.”

More specifically, users can access data for weeks, months, or non-calender intervals. This makes sense for application such as crop monitoring, where you’d like to see seasonal variation in the data:

“With Custom Satellite Embeddings, organizations can request custom data summaries tailored specifically to their areas of interest and timeframe, such as quarterly, monthly, weekly, or non-calendar-annual intervals down to a 5-day frequency (based on AlphaEarth Foundations input data sources). This enables businesses and public sector teams to shift from annual mapping to active, rolling monitoring and change detection, making it possible to monitor crop growth cycles, track climate-driven supply chain risks, and evaluate event-based damage after disasters occur.”

Many people mentioned he temporal limitation of Google’s Satellite Embeddings dataset, and this release provides a solution to that problem. Interested users can sign up for early access, this is feature is not yet publicly available.

Resource 3: MCP Apps, Connectors, and Plugins in-depth

If you’re new to GeoAI, you’ve probably heard the terms MCP servers, connectors, and plugins. But what do these terms mean'? This resource from the “Build to Launch” Substack explains in normal English what are the differences between all three and how they should be approached from a user perspective.

The takeaway is this:

item.title: Geospatial Analysis @ CARTO with PlacePulse embeddings and Google’s Satellite embeddings dataset
item.description: CARTO integrated Google’s satellite embeddings dataset into CARTO Workflows. They also just announced their own embeddings named PlacePulse.
item.dc:creator: Eric van Rees
item.content:encoded:
Resource 1: Geospatial AI with Google AlphaEarth Foundation Models and CARTO

The first resource is a webinar hosted by CARTO earlier this year. It features a short presentation from Earth Engine Solutions Scientist Katelyn Tarrio on Google’s Satellite embeddings, followed by a demo of how you can use them with CARTO Workflows, a visual, no-code/low-code tool used to design, automate, and run multi-step spatial analyses and data transformation pipelines.

What are Google Satellite embeddings?

Google Deepmind released AlphaEarth Foundations in June 2025. AlphaEarth Foundations integrates petabytes of earth observation data including optical and thermal imagery, radar, LiDAR, and climate data to create an embedding. Embeddings are learned compact feature vectors that summarize complex high-dimensional spatial, temporal, and multi-source data into low-dimensional space where the distance or similarity is meaningful.

GeoAI Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

AlphaEarth Foundations has been run at scale across the globe to produce the Google Satellite embeddings dataset which is a global data set of precomputed information-rich features that are analysis-ready. The embeddings have been packaged and summarized into 64 dimensional representations or bands similarly at a 10-meter spatial resolution for every year back to 2017.

What can you do with Google’s Satellite embeddings dataset?

The Google Satellite embeddings dataset can be used as a replacement for traditional raw imagery and complex hand-engineered features. Data scientists can perform all standard analyses including classification, regression, and change detection, but with the added benefit of achieving higher accuracy with significantly less training data than traditional methods because of the low-noise embedding space the model has created, which means fewer training points are needed to acheive the same or better high-quality results.

Similarity search is another application where the globe is scanned to find all locations with a similar surface and environmental conditions to the embedding space. The demo features an example of a similarity search, where a classification model to predict wildfires in California is used to identify areas resembling high-risk regions in Arizona. Watch the webinar below:

Resource 2: Turning Geospatial Foundation Models into Decisions using CARTO Workflows

Lucia Garcia Duarte, who presented the webinar listed above, also published an informative blog post explaining what are foundation models and how they can be used with CARTO Workflows for visualiziation, clustering, change detection, similarity searches, and traditional machine learning. The blog post is worth reading because of the examples she gives for each use case.

Resource 3: CARTO’s PlacePulse Embeddings

CARTO has just released its own embeddings. They were announced as follows:

This LinkedIn post links to a CARTO blog post, where it says that PlacePulse Embeddings provide a single vector for every location in the US that captures its overall profile (its people, economy, housing, commercial activity, and environmental characteristics), ready to compare, cluster, and predict from.

Regarding the temporal and spatial dimenstions, we learn that PlacePulse combines detailed 2025 information on demographics, business activity, commuting, health, income, as well as climate and environmental risk”, and that there is an embedding for every populated H3 cell in the US: about 1.06 million hexagons of roughly 5 km² each (H3 resolution 7). The embeddings will be distributed through CARTO’s Data Observatory.

The most interesting part of the blog post discusses how these embeddings compare to other embeddings:

Geospatial foundation models today are typically built from one of three kinds of data.

The first is signals of human activity: where people move, how busy a place is through the day, foot traffic and visits to points of interest, commuting flows, and web-search interest. These models are very good at capturing the rhythm of a place — how it behaves hour by hour and season by season.

The second is satellite and street-level imagery (e.g. AlphaEarth, Clay, TESSERA), which captures the physical appearance of a place: land cover, building density, road networks, vegetation, water and terrain.

The third is the lasting, structural makeup of a place: its detailed demographics, business mix, built environment, and climate and environmental risk, at fine resolution and national scale.

These three families answer different questions and are strongest in combination. Activity models tell you how a place behaves; imagery tells you what it physically looks like; structural models tell you who lives and works there and how a community is composed. PlacePulse is built to capture that third signal, and to sit alongside the other two rather than replace them.

Read more about CARTO’s PlacePulse embeddings in this blog post and here.

item.title: GeoAI @ Overture, Zephr, and Niantic Spatial
item.description: This Substack article is about the Overture Maps Foundation and how their data helps organizations ground AI systems, and how Overture itself uses AI internally when preparing that data for release.
item.dc:creator: Eric van Rees
item.content:encoded:
This Substack article offers a small sample of GeoAI initiatives at Overture, a collaborative open-data initiative led by software developers, data experts, cartographic engineers, and product managers from dozens of Overture Maps Foundation member companies. They are very active in the field of GeoAI, and have very innovative and interesting projects going on that are worth covering.

Resource 1: Geoawesome’s panel discussion on AI & the spatial data paradox

TL;DR The video below has a lot of interesting AI content. You’ll learn how four organizations in the spatial domain use AI for their daily workflows and help customers solve business problems. You’ll also learn about what it cannot do and where a human-first approach is required.

Earlier this year I watched a video from Geoawesome’s Next Geo event called “The Spatial Data Paradox” with panel discussion on today’s key drivers of spatial data creation and part of last week’s The Next Geo event, organized by Geoawesome.

The central topic is how different organizations deal with ever-increasing data quality requirements from the market, which is a direct outcome of the industry producing more and better data.

Tory Smith, Director of Product Management at Niantic Spatial, offers a a great insights on what’s one of the biggest challenges of new players in the mapping platform market. He points out that it remains extremely difficult for new companies and open data initiatives to reach the point where a global map is simultaneously built, used, and updated by its users. “Accessibility and ease of use are essential if you want people to contribute to world models, for example, by offering a mobile 3D scanning app that is easy to use”, he adds.

The latter half of the video covers AI. Panel host Marc Prioleau asks all guests how they make use of AI inside of their organization and to rate how important AI is for their business.

Smith discusses his work at Niantic Spatial, a geospatial AI and spatial computing company with a core mission to help machines and AI understand, map, and interact with the physical world at scale. Formed in 2025, Niantic Spatial builds on a long history in spatial computing. Its founding team created Keyhole, the satellite imagery platform acquired by Google, which later evolved into Google Earth and Google Maps.

Niantic Spatial was also ahead of the curve in adopting spatial data formats and types that weren’t widely considered at the time by others, including phone-derived models and Gaussian splats.

The video ends with Overture CTO Amy Rose discussing how AI is used for quality-control of their massive spatial data sets that are used widely in the geospatial industry.

Watch the video here:

GeoAI Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Resource 2: Releasing Spatial Data for AI-generative Workflows

At the end of the conversation in the video, panel host Marc Prioleau asks all participants how they use AI in their organization. I decided to follow-up on that question and reached out to Overture CTO Amy Rose for an interview where she discusses her work at Overture and how AI is used for preparing a dataset that is used widely in the industry for grounding AI systems.

Here’s a snippet about the potential of AI and its limits that I found interesting:

GEO: You recently discussed how Overture uses AI internally for preparing its data releases. Could you please explain how this works, where you think AI makes a great use case, and where it doesn’t for you as a foundation?

Amy Rose: The processing and coding side is a given at this point. Machine learning has been part of how map data gets made for years, and some of our source data is machine generated. That’s real, but isn’t the most interesting part.

The interesting part is validation, and it is also where I am most cautious. You can automate a great deal and get output that looks plausible. You still have to benchmark it against something real, and ground level validation doesn’t get easier as volume goes up. It gets harder. That stays a human problem longer than people expect.

The other place AI doesn’t help is the part of this project that’s paramount and at the core of what we do. Deciding what goes into a release is not a technical question. It is getting the right people in the room, and you can’t just have engineers in the room. You need the conversation to cover product value, the business case and technical feasibility on a real timeline, and then reach consensus. No model does that for you.

A second cause for writing an article about Overture is that in July 2026, Overture announced it had reached 50 members, nearly double its 2024 count, as commercial, public-sector, academia and non-profit organizations standardize on open base-map data and its Global Entity Reference System (GERS).

From the accompanying press release: “the driver is AI grounding. Without a shared, stable reference for physical places, models and agents risk inventing storefronts, missing intersections, or routing people to businesses that closed years ago. GERS assigns every place, road and boundary a resolvable ID, enabling AI to anchor outputs to real-world entities instead of probabilistic guesses.”

You can read the interview with Amy Rose for GeoConnexion here.

Resource 3: How 10 AI Startups are Grounding AI in the Real World with Overture

The third resource is a blog article from Overture that discusses how 10 AI startups use Overture’s data. As stated in the article, AI models require a structured, verifiable grounding layer for spatial retrieval-augmented generation, which provides a trusted source of geospatial facts to prevent hallucinations. And this is where Overture’s spatial data comes into play.

On top of the list in the image above is Zephr. Overture published an extensive, separate blog post explaining how Zephr is collaborating with Overture to teach AI agents to understand the world around them, or, put differently, let an LLM understand place:

Zephr’s founding work was software that sharpens the data from the phone’s hardware to sub-meter accuracy and full orientation. For the challenge, Zephr created a system that converts surrounding spatial data into relationships a language model can reason over.

What started with a proposal to the Overture community to build a shared pipeline that uses street-level imagery to put places pins where businesses actually are, resulted in a Places Grounding service built on Overture data and exposed through MCP, the open protocol that lets AI assistants call external tools:

It’s live across the 49 largest metro areas in the United States, drawing on tens of millions of places. Nearly ten million of those places are enhanced with entrances, facades, and visual descriptions that are specific enough to recognize on sight […].

The piece also hints at future implications of Zephr’s project oucomes to let an LLM understand its surroundings:

Soon enough, navigating Boulder or London or Tokyo or Lagos won’t involve a screen at all. You’ll ask, your assistant will answer and guide you, and the map underneath will finally know where the front doors are. Not a map you look at. A map you move through.

That’s it for this week!

item.title: Introducing Geospatial MCP Servers
item.description: This week’s article contains three resources on geospatial MCP servers, explaining what are MCP servers, how do they provide GeoAI capabilities to its users, and where to find them?
item.dc:creator: Eric van Rees
item.content:encoded:
Resource 1: A very short introduction to MCP Servers

If you’re new to GeoAI, you’ve probably heard about MCP Servers. I first heard about them earlier this year in a webinar from GeoAwesome. The first resource from this article is a short video that explains what are MCP servers without any technical jargon. Long story short: MCP servers add a layer to an LLM to connect with other services. The idea is to provide an LLM with a tool so it can perform a task instead of producing text (which is its primary task).

Another takeway from the video below is that MCP servers are nothing new (except for the term itself). In other words, during the last two years it was already possible to connect LLM with other tools and have it perform specific tasks for you (say, send an email through Gmail).

Thanks for reading GeoAI Signal! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Some additional info on the acronym MCP: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for AI tools to connect with external services. Within the context of geospatial AI, this connection enables agents to consult APIs, databases, and files that provide the geographical context required to solve spatial problems. Such consultation (also known as ‘grounding’) is a necessary step to make sure an AI model is “anchored” to a source of truth.

Resource 2: Felt’s AI agent that fetches data, runs spatial queries and builds maps

This brings me to the second resource, which is a presentation of Felt’s agentic AI-native GIS & mapping platform. This 16-minute video is a great example of an MCP server (also described as an ‘AI agent’) that acts as a layer between an LLM, a databricks data warehouse, and Felt’s set of spatial subfunctions that extend that same data warehouse.

As Felt noticed that LLMs cannot answer spatial questions, it wanted to make sure its GIS solution is cloud-native by default, where the browser is the default interface, and natural language (= prompting) is the starting point when opening up the application. Its GIS agent builds on top of DataBricks and any other cloud system, instead of treating GIS as a secondary source of truth.

The MCP Server is part of a larger platform GIS and mapping platform for building maps and dashboards:

Felt’s MCP server is available through in the databricks Marketplace, and can be installed from there:

The MCP server contains 30+ GIS specific capabilities which LLMs by default cannot do. A selection of these are outlined below inside the red-marked box:

With the MCP server installed, humans can now write a prompt with a spatial question directed to an AI agent inside Slack, which triggers a set of prompts, runs those in the background, and returns the results to the user:

Behind the scenes, the AI agent starts looking for the right data inside and outside the data warehouse, and performs spatial analysis, maps the results, and returns a text prompt with the results to answer the user’s initial question (see the red-marked box):

I think this product demo is a great example of modern-day, cloud-based and agentic GIS. An MCP server connects and LLM with GIS tools to prepare and perform spatial analysis, with a human operator validating the results, inputs, and process (workflow). This is probably the next phase of GIS analysis, and the follow-up to desktop GIS.

Resource 3: A Github repo with Geospatial MCP servers

The following LinkedIn post showed up in my daily feed recently:

It links to a Github repo of geospatial MCPs. As stated below, it contains a curated, tracked list of Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for geospatial, GIS, mapping, and earth-observation work, including geocoding, routing, PostGIS, STAC/imagery, QGIS/ArcGIS, weather, and the commercial location platforms.

This is a handy repo as there’s no coordinated effort among vendors or other stakeholders to MCP development:

That’s it for this week!

Thanks for reading GeoAI Signal! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

item.title: Start Here: GeoAI Signal
item.description: The newsletter about what’s new in geospatial artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Eric van Rees
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to GeoAI Signal.

If you’re interested in how artificial intelligence is changing geospatial technology and how geospatial data is changing what AI can do, you’re in the right place.

GeoAI is evolving quickly. New models, research papers, datasets, tools, platforms, and applications are emerging constantly. It can be difficult to keep up, and even harder to know which developments are genuinely important.

GeoAI Signal is my attempt to make that easier.

I curate and annotate the developments I think are worth knowing about, so you can spend less time searching through the noise and more time understanding the signal.

What is GeoAI Signal?

GeoAI Signal is a weekly publication focused on the intersection of geospatial technology and artificial intelligence.

I look across research, industry, open-source projects, datasets, models, tools, and emerging applications to identify developments that could shape the future of GeoAI.

The emphasis isn’t simply on what’s new: it’s on what’s interesting, what matters, and what might come next.

I also want to stress that it’s not primarily about technology, but about humans interacting with technology. Many companies use AI to replace humans, but that’s a completely wrong take: AI is made to be used by humans, not to replace them. It’s the combination of technology and the human element that interests me, not technology by itself.

This means that I will be citing from human creators and writing for a human audience. There are many great content creators putting out content (videos, articles, podcasts) that deserve to be shared more widely. In the old days, geospatial media were the platform to do this but today’s world is a little more fragmented. Substack provides an opportunity to write and distribute content easily, which is why I chose to use it. I see it as an improvement to Medium.com which is problematic as so much content is gated today.

The idea is to share 1-3 great resources with you and share my thoughts on them. Over the last few months, I wrote a lot of LinkedIn posts about GeoAI and got a lot of response. This told me there was a greater opportunity waiting, which resulted in this Substack publication.

Who is this for?

GeoAI Signal is for anyone who wants to understand where geospatial AI is going.

That includes:

  • GIS and geospatial professionals

  • Remote sensing and Earth observation practitioners

  • Researchers and academics

  • Data scientists and AI/ML practitioners

  • Technology leaders and strategists

  • Developers and entrepreneurs

  • Students and people entering the field

  • Anyone curious about the intersection of AI and geography

You don’t need to be an AI researcher or a geospatial expert.

My goal is to make important developments accessible while still providing enough technical and strategic context to make them useful.

What you’ll get each week

For free subscribers, the core of GeoAI Signal is simple:

3 annotated resources every week

Each week I’ll select three resources that I think are worth your attention.

They might be:

  • A new research paper

  • A new geospatial AI model

  • A dataset or benchmark

  • An open-source project

  • A new tool or platform

  • An interesting application

  • A significant industry development

Or an emerging idea that I think deserves more attention

But I won’t simply send you three links.

I’ll add context and commentary explaining why I selected each resource, what I find interesting about it, and what it might tell us about the direction of the field.

The objective is straightforward: less noise, more signal.

My point of view

I’m interested in GeoAI not simply as another application of AI, but as a meeting point between two rapidly changing fields.

Geospatial data has always provided a way to understand our physical world. AI is changing how we collect, process, analyze, model, and interact with that data.

That creates enormous opportunities, but also plenty of hype.

So I’m going to try to maintain a few principles:

  • Curious, but skeptical: new technology can be exciting without necessarily being transformative.

  • Focused on substance: I’ll prioritize useful research, tools, ideas, and developments over hype and announcements.

  • Looking beyond the obvious: The most interesting GeoAI developments aren’t always the ones getting the most attention.

  • Connecting the dots: a single paper or model can be interesting. A pattern emerging across many developments is much more interesting.

Ultimately, I’m trying to answer a simple question:

What should people who care about geospatial AI be paying attention to right now?

I’ve already published several pieces to get GeoAI Signal underway. These give you an idea of what to expect: annoted news about embeddings, MCP servers, AI agents, voice-based assistants, new use cases, startups, courses and other resources.

If you’re new here, these are the 3–5 articles I’d recommend starting with:

  1. A Beginner’s Guide to Geo AI

Provides a short, high-level overview of what the term means and why it’s important.

  1. What is geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI)?

A slightly longer introduction of GeoAI, and a practical example.

  1. Beyond Maps: How Geospatial AI Creates Competitive Advantage

Explains how organizations can implement GeoAI and different industries leverage it.

  1. What’s GeoAI? How AI enhances GIS and geospatial data analytics

Differentiates between five types of geospatial intelligence and key components that enable it.

  1. What Is GeoAI — and Why Does It Matter?

A LinkedIn post that explains how GeoAI forms part of a bigger picture, what it can do, and wich challenges remain.

I’ll update this section as the publication grows, so it can serve as a running guide to some of the most useful work published here.

What paid subscribers get

The free newsletter is designed to keep you informed.

Paid subscriptions are for going deeper.

Paid subscribers get access to exclusive content, insights, resources, and reports designed for readers who want a more detailed view of where GeoAI is heading and how it is evolving.

That means more than simply getting additional links.

I’ll use the paid edition to spend more time on:

  • In-depth analysis of important GeoAI developments

  • Original insights and commentary

  • Detailed explorations of emerging technologies and trends

  • Curated resources and collections

  • Reports and briefings on important areas of the field

  • The connections and implications that aren’t always obvious from the headlines

The goal is to build something increasingly useful over time: a deeper source of analysis and reference material for understanding GeoAI.

Why I started GeoAI Signal

I started GeoAI Signal because the amount of interesting work happening at the intersection of AI and geospatial technology is growing incredibly quickly.

There are new papers to read, models to evaluate, tools to try, datasets to explore, companies to watch, and applications to understand.

But information abundance creates its own problem.

Finding information isn’t the same as understanding what’s important.

I wanted to create a place where I could continuously collect, filter, explore, and share the developments that I find most interesting—and build a record of how the field evolves along the way.

That’s what GeoAI Signal is.

A weekly signal through the noise.

If that sounds useful, subscribe for free and get the three annotated GeoAI resources each week.

And if you want to go deeper, become a paid subscriber and support the research behind the publication while getting access to the exclusive analysis, insights, resources, and reports.

Thanks for being here.

Eric van Rees

item.title: GeoAI: Birth, Evolution, and Recent Practical Examples
item.description: In my third article on Substack, I share three resources with practical GeoAI examples and some historical background for a better understanding of how we got to where we are today.
item.dc:creator: Eric van Rees
item.content:encoded:
Resource 1: The Birth and Evolution of GeoAI

If you thought that the term GeoAI is recent, you’d be surprised to read this article describing the birth and evolution of GeoAI. Written in 2020 (!), it examines how GeoAI evolved over time, starting in the 1950s.


Author Anastassios Dardas defines GeoAI as follows:

“GeoAI is a highly interdisciplinary field that links several applied scientific fields including computer science, engineering, statistics and spatial science with geographic theory.”

He writes that GeoAI has its roots as early as the mid-1960s, and considers a timeline with four generations of GeoAI developments. He argues that simultaneous advancement in the following seven key drivers have defined the evolution of GeoAI from its roots in the 1950s:

Thanks for reading GeoAI Signal! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

  1. Hardware technologies

  2. Access and availability of data

  3. Level of connectivity

  4. Machine Learning technologies

  5. Software technologies

  6. GIS roles

  7. Output

The mid-1960s to late-1990s mark the first 1st generation of GeoAI, which was defined by limitations in computational power and the restrictions of data availability and accessibility, which constrained the full use of machine learning algorithms.

The second GeoAI generation from 2000 to late-2000s is defined by the entrance into the Web era and early implementation of enterprise solutions. The years 2010 – 2019 marked “exponential growth in use by government agencies, corporations, NGOs, and academics to solve real world spatial problems” as well as significant breakthroughs in GIS, ML, storage and computational technologies, and widespread availability and accessibility of data.

The fourth wave of GeoAI started in 2020, which marked a transition from an era of collecting and processing “big” data to automatic informed decision-making processes driven by “intelligent” systems with little to no human intervention. The author was right in predicting “widespread use of generative adversarial networks (GANs), reinforcement learning, and transfer learning” (refer to the Machine Learning entry under the header 4th Generation of GeoAI (2020 - ?): The Frontier of Intelligence).

The author’s prediction about the changing role of the GIS analyst in today’s job market in some way anticipates the geospatial embeddings now offered by major GIS vendors following Google’s example:

“…the GeoAI scientist will be expected to have a strong GIS background while, at the same time, performing the duties of a data scientist including the creation of DL [Deep Learning] and semantic models within the spatial dimension.”

Resource 2: A Breakdown of Geographic Embeddings

The following video explains very well what are embeddings are and how you can use them. Matt Forrest and Qiusheng Wu provide an excellent introduction to the AlphaEarth Foundations release and its embeddings, leaving out many of the distracting technical details behind how they work. (If you don’t want to watch the entire video but are only intersted in the embeddings part, skip to 22:30.)

The video was recorded right after AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) was released by Google DeepMind, a foundation model used to produce geographic embeddings. AEF made it possible to "catalogue" the Earth both spatially and temporally in 10 × 10 metre cells for each year between 2017 and 2025. Every cell stores a 64-dimensional embedding vector (a list of 64 numbers).

Until the release of AEF, nothing quite like it was publicly available. For the first time, there was a temporally and spatially consistent dataset covering the entire Earth over multiple consecutive years. AEF’s embeddings can be used much like a regular imagery dataset, so there is no need to train your own foundation model before using them. This significantly lowered the barrier to working with satellite imagery, although users should be aware of the dataset’s spatial and temporal limitations.

For example, each embedding represents an entire year’s worth of observations rather than monthly or weekly snapshots. As a result, it is not possible to detect seasonal agricultural changes throughout the year.

The spatial and temporal limitations of AEF’s embeddings

The temporal resolution also means that the embeddings are only available for the years in which they were generated (2017–2025). It is unlikely that comparable embeddings will become available for years before 2017 because there are insufficient consistent satellite observations from earlier periods to create annual global representations. There is also a spatial limitation: with a resolution of 10 × 10 metres, the embeddings are generally too coarse for applications such as detecting individual buildings in satellite imagery.

Even with these limitations, the embeddings are well suited to many downstream applications, including supervised and unsupervised classification, clustering, similarity analysis, and change detection.

One practical challenge when working with embeddings is the sheer size of the dataset. Depending on the terrain they represent, the downloadable GeoTIFF files range from approximately 0.8 GB to 3.5 GB. For many users, it makes more sense to access the data through Google Earth Engine using JavaScript or Python than to download the files locally.

Although the advantages of embeddings are clear (they are freely available and require no model training) the question remains whether they are the best choice when so much Earth observation data is already available. It is important to understand what embeddings can and cannot do (at least for now). Both Dr. Qiusheng Wu and Matt Forrest point out that current-generation embeddings are not suitable for object detection. Instead, they excel at identifying patterns, measuring similarity, detecting change, and supporting other large-scale geospatial analyses.

Resource 3: How to build a JS web app with AI

I came across this recent article from Agnieszka Rozniak at Esri’s ArcGIS Blog. Agnieszka used the ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript with agentic coding to build a web app. The idea stems from curiousity, as she writes at the end of the article:

“My goal with the Malbork Castle Explorer was to see whether agentic AI could help turn an idea, available data, and an initial UX concept into a functional prototype.”

This article provides a lot of great advice for setting up and running a small spatial web app, including:

  1. how to use AI to document creating a geospatial web app

  2. how to prompt agentic AI to build a geospatial web app from scratch

  3. how to revert back to earlier generated code when new code or code changes do not result in the expected outcome

  4. how to test and refine AI-generated outputs.

Much of the article describes the process of creating the app and interacting with agentic AI (GitHub Copilot in this case), moving back and forth between generated output and what she expected:

“When an issue appeared to stem from a misunderstanding, I would often ask AI to review the original prompts and identify potential ambiguities. This often helped me spot gaps in my thinking and rephrase the requests more clearly.”

She also used AI to generate project documentation, which in turn served as input for AI for testing and refinement:

“I asked AI to compare the implementation against the project’s original technical constraints and point out anything that didn’t match the documented approach.”

When AI-generated code changes didn’t result in the expected outcome, she’d use code versions generated at an earlier stage:

“Regular commits to GitHub provided an additional safety net and made it easy to return to earlier versions when needed.”

She stresses the importance of giving AI as much context as possible before starting out, which made for a smoother app creation process:

“Looking back, giving AI context was one of the most important parts of the workflow. The most helpful prompt was not simply “build an app.” It was the information around the app: what I wanted to create, which technologies to use, what to avoid, where the data came from, and how I wanted AI to collaborate with me.”

Finally, the concludes that AI is not a substitute for critical thinking:

“The biggest lesson from this project was that AI worked best when I treated it as a collaborator, not as an autopilot. It could generate code, suggest implementation plans, and help debug issues, but I still needed to define the goal, test the result, and decide which recommendations to accept.”

That’s it for this week!

item.title: How GeoAI is Changing Modern GIS Jobs and Education
item.description: In my second Substack post, I share two resources that discuss how GeoAI is changing the geospatial job market and academic education.
item.dc:creator: Eric van Rees
item.content:encoded:
GeoAI is changing the profession of the spatial analyst. This means that anyone looking for a job in modern GIS is expected to manage AI tools and technology, but up to a point. This is one of the takeways of Matt Forrest’s recent video “The FASTEST Way to Learn GIS in 2026 (and ACTUALLY Get a Job)”:

In the video, he outlines the four must-have skills to find a modern GIS job:

Thanks for reading GeoAI Signal! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

In addition to this, he discusses the role of AI in modern GIS and comes to the conclusion that while it’s important, it’s not a separate skill, but rather one that enhances the four basic skills. I wrote down the following quote from his video:

“You might have noticed I didn’t list AI as a separate tool. That is intentional. AI is not a tool in your toolkit. It’s a layer that accelerates every other tool you’re using. Claude connects to QGIS through MCP. Claude Code can help you write Python or debug a SQL query. It is a force multiplier but it cannot multiply your existing knowledge. Learn the stack first, then add AI on top, not the other way around.“

I other words, AI can never replace human thinking or decision-making, but rather accelerate workflows of those with strong skills required in modern GIS. Later in the video, he expands on this by explaning why prompting isn’t the same thing as learning:

“Prompting isn’t learning. You need to be able to explain every line an LLM returns when you ask it to write a SQL query for you. If you cannot do this, you don’t understand it. Learn the fundamentals manually first, write your own queries by hand. Hit the walls, struggle through the debugging, build the muscle memory. Do not use AI during the first 20 hours of learning any new tool. After those first 20 hours, bring in AI as a collaborator, not as a crutch. “

He concludes his throughts on AI with the following statement:

“AI is not replacing GIS, AI is replacing the people that never learned what they were doing in the first place.”

The second resource I’m sharing this week is an article from GeoAwesome written by Aleks Buczkowski, “How AI will Reshape the Geospatial Job Market”. The author not only describes which skills are required for geospatial jobs today, but also how geospatial education is changing as a result of changing technology. Aleks has a unique perspective as he also hires juniors for geospatial jobs in his current job. The article makes for an interesting comparison with Matt Forrest’s video, as both authors share overlapping topics but from a different perspective.

For example, Forrest stresses the importance of visualization skills of spatial analysis. He distinguishes cartography and dashboards as two important tools to communicate the results of spatial analysis, which require different technologies. Being able to communicate with non-spatial experts is crucial inside organizations where there’s a single spatial data analyst at work.

With regards to AI, Buczkowski seems to agree with Forrest that it cannot replace critical thinking, reasoning, and communication. This is displayed in a graphic that sums up different human skills AI can’t replicate. What AI can do, however, is automate parts of a larger system:

“[…] GIS is not one task. It is a system for representing place, integrating evidence and supporting decisions. AI can automate components of that system, sometimes dramatically, without assuming responsibility for the system as a whole. […] The important workforce question is therefore not whether a professional can use AI. It is whether that person can supervise an increasingly automated spatial process.”

That’s it for this week!

Let me do the searching for you

As many professionals in the geospatial industry are looking for ways to level up, I thought it would be a good idea to start a Substack on GeoAI content. Not only to document my own learning path, but to share great finds with others.

What I don’t want to do is a send out a list of random links - there are enough people who do this already.

So why subscribe?

  1. I spend a lot of time online searching for news and content. I know where to find it so you don’t have to.

  2. I have been working in the industry for 20+ years, so I know who are the content creators you need to follow, and where to find great content.

  3. Let’s face it: LinkedIn is going downhill quickly. You need to wade through a lot of trash to get to the good stuff. Skip the TikTok reels, selfies, and sales pitches by subscribing to my Substack as I’ve down the dirty work for you.

Still here? Great. Let’s start with the basics. These links will help you get started on your GeoAI journey right away.

  1. New to AI? No worries. This free 3-hour video course on AI agents will teach you how they’re different from LLMs and how to create one using Python.

  2. Are you GIS user looking for a book that teaches you how to use GeoAI in your daily work? Esri just published Exploring GeoAI: Tools and Workflows, a practical guide to applying geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) using ArcGIS. Read the press announcement here.

  3. Geolytix created a 6-part podcast with Ed Parsons on location intelligence and AI, which promises “cutting through the hype to find real clarity”.
